performers: Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra; Fritz Reiner, conductor
intro: An oboe tune and a broad viola song are enjoying themselves when a clarinet barges in with a march from Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony. The trombones answer with a pair of rude slides.

sections.label: A · Oboe song, uneven steps
sections.mNote: The oboe sings across changing metres and plucked string notes

sections.label: B · Violas sing over harps
sections.mNote: Calmo: a broad viola melody, then violins and cor anglais

sections.label: A′ · The oboe song returns
sections.mNote: Flute and clarinet join the oboe over plucked bass notes

sections.label: X · Clarinet march, trombone jeers
sections.mNote: A borrowed march accelerates into brass slides and wind chatter

sections.label: B′ · The song returns with mutes
sections.mNote: Muted violins and violas sing over harp chords

sections.label: A″ · Oboe, flute and clarinet
sections.mNote: The first tune passes between solo winds

sections.label: Coda · A little flute cadenza
sections.mNote: The flute lingers over held horns and strings

cues.title: An uneven little song
cues.text: After a short string introduction, the oboe sings a tune whose bars keep changing length. Plucked viola and cello notes put small bumps in its path.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, plate B. & H. 9009, p. 68: opening string chords, oboe tune and changing metres: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violas sing out
cues.text: Calmo: the violas have a broad, singing melody, with two harps supplying the chords. The violins take it up, and the cor anglais joins them. For a while, everybody has time to finish a sentence.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 70, printed bars 42–58: Calmo, viola cantabile, two harps, then violins and cor anglais. Printed bar numbers count the opening upbeat: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An uninvited march
cues.text: The clarinet brings in the march tune from Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony. The strings hurry it along, and the brass breaks in. Then the trombones slide upwards: an orchestral raspberry.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 72–73, printed bars 75–92: clarinet tune, accelerando and trombone glissandi. Richard E. Rodda identifies the Shostakovich quotation in the Pittsburgh Symphony programme of January 2020: https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Whose joke is it?
cues.text: Bartók’s march parodies the “invasion” theme of Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony, which itself refers to “Da geh’ ich zu Maxim” from Lehár’s operetta The Merry Widow. Whether Bartók mocks Shostakovich, Lehár or both has been argued ever since.
cues.evidence: Richard Rodda, Pittsburgh Symphony programme note, 17–19 January 2020: the interruption parodies the German march theme of the first movement of Shostakovich’s Seventh Symphony, itself a mocking phrase from Lehár’s The Merry Widow. https://culturaldistrict-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/culturaldistrict/system/assets/29105/original/Jan._17-19__2020.pdf. Berlin Philharmonic programme note (the Lehár melody woven with Shostakovich’s invasion theme): https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/bela-bartok-concerto-for-orchestra-sz-116. Which is the target is argued in letters to The Guardian, 4 January 2016: https://www.theguardian.com/music/2016/jan/04/another-theory-on-bela-bartok-send-up-in-concerto-for-orchestra

cues.title: The song after the commotion
cues.text: The broad song returns in muted violins and violas, over harp chords and plucked lower strings. Bartók writes non crescendo as it rises. It keeps its voice down.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 76, Calmo, printed bars 119–127: muted strings, harp, pizzicato accompaniment and non crescendo: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ballet left on paper
cues.text: In January 1944 Bartók signs a contract for a ballet version of the concerto with American Ballet Theatre. He prepares a piano score; the conductor Antal Doráti helps with the negotiations. The ballet never reaches the stage.
cues.evidence: Klára Móricz, Comments to the critical edition, source A-piano: contract signed on 6 January 1944; piano reduction and unperformed ballet. https://www.henle.de/media/7c/05/ab/1697725629/7001-1697725628-sync.pdf

cues.title: The flute takes its time
cues.text: A little flute cadenza loosens the beat. Horns and strings hold their notes underneath while the flute turns back on itself, pauses and runs on. The final exchanges are short and quiet.
cues.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 77–78: rallentando, fermatas, quasi Cadenza and the closing a tempo: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Violas take the longer phrase
transitions.how: The flute and oboe finish their short phrases. At Calmo, the violas begin a melody marked cantabile, with two harps striking chords beneath it. The cellos and double basses fall silent for the first stretch; timpani supply the low notes.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 70, printed bars 38–50: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The oboe recovers its tune
transitions.how: The harp chords stop as the broad song ends. At Tempo I, the oboe resumes the opening tune, with flute and clarinet answering it. Violins and violas hold chords; plucked cellos and double basses keep the accompaniment light.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 71, from the Tempo I after printed bar 59: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The clarinet brings a march
transitions.how: Repeated string figures start beneath a held horn note; the cellos and basses pluck their accompaniment. The clarinet introduces the march. An accelerando carries it into Più mosso, where muted trumpet and trombone chords cut across it. Two upward trombone slides follow.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 72–73, printed bars 75–92: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: Mutes soften the returning song
transitions.to: B′ · The song returns with mutes
transitions.how: The wind chatter dwindles and the tuba holds its last note. The Calmo song returns in muted violins and violas. Harp chords and plucked second violins, cellos and double basses accompany it; Bartók asks the rising phrase to remain quiet.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, p. 76, Calmo and non crescendo, printed bars 119–127: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The strings leave the winds alone
transitions.from: B′ · The song returns with mutes
transitions.how: The oboe begins its old tune over the last harp and string chord. The accompaniment drops out. Flute, oboe and clarinet exchange short phrases alone before the strings rejoin them at Tempo I.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 76–77, printed bars 127–136: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

transitions.title: The flute stretches the beat
transitions.how: A slowing phrase and a fermata leave room for the flute. Its quasi Cadenza runs over held horn and string chords, with the double basses silent. The score allows the flautist to repeat a small turn freely before a descending run and the return to a tempo.
transitions.evidence: Boosey & Hawkes full score, pp. 77–78: quasi Cadenza, rubato and più volte ad libitum above the flute figure: https://www.imslp.eu/autoindex/index.php?dir=euimg/c/c4/&file=IMSLP19114-PMLP04854-Bart%C3%B3k_-_Concerto_for_Orchestra_%28orch._score%29.pdf

source.title: Bartók, Concerto for Orchestra, B. & H. 9009, IV
source.locator: Boosey & Hawkes full score, printed pp. 68–78: oboe and viola songs, the clarinet interruption and the closing flute cadenza. The printed bar numbers count the opening upbeat.

timeline.note: The oboe sings over strings, with plucked viola and cello notes (p. 68).
The tune passes between flute and oboe, with clarinet and bassoon replies over strings (pp. 68–70).
Violas begin the Calmo song over harps and timpani; violins and cor anglais take it up (p. 70).
The oboe’s first tune returns, with flute and clarinet replies above plucked bass notes (pp. 71–72).
The clarinet march meets brass chords, trombone slides and chattering winds (pp. 72–75).
Muted violins and violas recover the Calmo song over harp chords and plucked strings (p. 76).
The first tune passes between solo winds; the strings fall silent, then rejoin them (pp. 76–77).
The flute plays a little cadenza above held horns and strings before the last short phrases (p. 78).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending.
fields.note: Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The critical edition identifies this range for the complete recording. The Sony discographical transcription gives 5 February for CD 5 tracks 1–5; individual movement/session allocation is not established. Neither the 1948 issue nor 2010 upload is a session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue stated in the reproduced Columbia session discography. No microphone position or engineer is established for the selected transfer.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: This identifies the original commercial recording, not the unidentified physical or digital carrier from which the Archive MP3 was copied.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The discographical transcription dates MM-793 to 22 November 1948 and ML 4102 to 7 February 1949. Douglas Watt’s March 1949 review independently identifies Columbia set 793 and ML-4102 as the same Pittsburgh/Reiner performance. The exact carrier used by public-domain-archive.com remains unknown; no sleeve or label scans accompany the selected Archive item.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Complete set: XCO 35800–35811, take 1; LP matrices xLP 539 (I–II), xLP 540 (III–V)
fields.note: These are complete-recording identifiers transcribed from Sony’s discography, not an asserted side-by-side mapping for this MP3. Individual movement matrix boundaries, transfer-side joins and the transferred pressing are unknown. DAHR’s opened Reiner listing does not include these Columbia masters; no DAHR matrix record is fabricated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: Archive says only that the files were taken from public-domain-archive.com. Neither transfer engineer nor restoration producer is named. The uploader is not treated as the transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive public date, 8 August 2010, and file modification dates describe repository activity, not the date of analogue transfer or mastering.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original digitisation, equalisation, noise reduction, editing, speed correction and the source carrier are unestablished. The item calls the selected file an original VBR MP3 and supplies Ogg derivatives; this does not identify how the historical master was transferred.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in the EU under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; not a worldwide clearance.
fields.note: Bartók died in 1945; IMSLP identifies this score as public domain in life-plus-70 countries and explicitly warns of continuing US protection. The critical-edition commentary is cited as scholarship, not redistributed as a public-domain score.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963.
fields.note: Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: He heard a future for concert music in village songs, and went out with a phonograph to learn how they were sung.
facts: István Thomán, a Liszt pupil, and Hans Koessler; Budapest Academy, 1899–1903
Piano professor in Budapest, 1907–34; folk-music research in Budapest and at Columbia University
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages; Biskra, 1913; Turkey with Adnan Saygun, 1936
Six quartets, three piano concertos, two violin concertos, three stage works and Mikrokosmos
composer.background:
In May 1904 Bartók went to stay with the Fischer family at Gerlicepuszta. He had a piano sent out, practised four hours a day and composed for four or five more. There he heard Lidi Dósa, a young woman from Transylvania in the family’s service, singing to the children in her care, and began writing down her songs. Here was Hungarian music unlike the urban entertainment that usually went by that name, and he wanted more of it. Two years later, collecting with Bartók, the writer Béla Balázs found that the frail-looking pianist could wear him out: “I was already very tired, but he kept urging and driving me on to collect more!” Balázs put the encounter in his diary.

Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós in 1881, when the town belonged to Hungary; it is now Sânnicolau Mare in Romania. His father, director of an agricultural school, died when he was seven. His mother Paula supported Béla and his sister by teaching, moving between towns before settling in Pozsony, now Bratislava. At the Budapest Academy he studied piano with István Thomán, who had studied with Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler.
